title: Running the Provinces
objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.
summary: Governors ran provinces, split by Augustus between the Senate and himself. Taxes came from a census, and local elites did most of the work.

cards.headline: Rome ran a vast empire with surprisingly few officials.
cards.body: So who did all the work? Mostly, other people.

cards.headline: Who got which province
cards.body: Augustus split the provinces in two. Peaceful ones got governors chosen by the Senate. Frontier provinces, the ones with armies, were run by his own deputies. Notice which half he kept: the half with the soldiers. Either way, every province paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation. Being counted by Rome meant being charged by Rome.

cards.headline: Local help
cards.body: Here’s the few-officials secret. Rome relied on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes. Under the Republic, tax collection had often been contracted out to private companies of publicani instead, and they were notorious for abuses. Handing a for-profit company the job of squeezing your subjects: what could go wrong?

cards.fact: Pontius Pilate was a provincial governor.
cards.context: He was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. A name most people know, in a job most people never think about.

cards.headline: The provinces: run
learned: Local elites did most of the governing

questions.prompt: Who collected taxes for Rome in many Republican provinces?
questions.explanation: Tax collection was often contracted out to publicani, notorious for abuses.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus keep the frontier provinces for himself?

options.label: That was where the armies were
The Senate refused to govern them

questions.explanation: Frontier provinces held the legions, and controlling them meant controlling the army.

questions.prompt: From Level 30: which was Rome’s first province?
questions.explanation: Rome’s provinces began with Sicily, taken after the First Punic War.
